1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 15:32.
See how you translated this expression in 9:9, where it has a similar meaning. Alternate translation: [the servant of Mephibosheth]

The expression **saddled** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [donkeys that someone had saddled]
Here, **summer fruit** represents “figs.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and 100 bunches of figs]

2.note: David is using **What {are} these to you?** as a common expression of his culture to mean “Why have you brought these things?” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What do you have here] or [Why have you brought these things]

Even though Ziba is addressing David directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **the king** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [for your house]
Ziba is using the term **house** to mean David’s household, that is, his family and servants. Alternate translation: [for the household of the king] or [for your household]

Ziba is using the adjective **faint** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [is for people who become faint in the wilderness]

3.q: יוֹשֵׁ֣ב בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֔ם כִּ֣י אָמַ֔ר הַ⁠יּ֗וֹם יָשִׁ֤יבוּ לִ⁠י֙ בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֵ֖ת מַמְלְכ֥וּת אָבִֽ⁠י
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since he said, ‘Today, the house of Israel will return the kingdom of my father to me,’ he is staying in Jerusalem]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:7. Alternate translation: [my grandfather]

4.note: Ziba did **prostrate** himself as he said this. This was a symbolic action that expressed submission, respect, and gratitude to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I prostrate myself to you in submission and gratitude]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:19. Alternate translation: [May you regard me with favor]

5.q: מִ⁠שָּׁם֩ אִ֨ישׁ יוֹצֵ֜א מִ⁠מִּשְׁפַּ֣חַת בֵּית־שָׁא֗וּל וּ⁠שְׁמ⁠וֹ֙ שִׁמְעִ֣י בֶן־גֵּרָ֔א
5.note: Here the author is introducing Shimei as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain man named Shimei son of Gera, who belonged to the same clan as Saul’s family, was coming out from there]

The phrase **coming out and cursing** expresses a single idea. The word **cursing** tells in what way Shimei was **coming out**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [and he was cursing as he came out]

6.note: It might seem that the expression **stoned David with stones** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And he hurled stones at David]

Throwing stones at David was a symbolic action by which Shimei showed contempt and rebellion against David’s authority as king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [he contemptuously threw stones at David]

The author is using this clause to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for the event that he describes in the first part of the verse. Connect this clause to that event in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing at the same time. Alternate translation: [even though all of the people and all of the mighty had formed a protective shield on his right and on his left]

The author is using the adjective **mighty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the mighty warriors]

The author is referring to the area all around David by naming two directions, **on his right** and **on his left**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [were surrounding him]

7.note: Shimei is repeating the verb **get out** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Get all the way out of here]

Shimei is saying **man of** here in the same way that biblical authors and characters often use the similar expression “son of” to indicate that a person has the characteristic of something. In this case, Shimei is saying that David has the characteristics of being deadly violent and wicked. The first phrase describes what David has done, and the second phrase describes what kind of person Shimei believes David to be. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

The word **blood** is plural here because it refers to blood shed by violence. Your language may use the plural form of its word for blood to mean the same thing. If not, you could express the meaning in another way, here and in the next verse. See how you translated the similar expression in 3:28. Alternate translation: [man of bloodshed]

8.q: הֵשִׁיב֩ עָלֶ֨י⁠ךָ יְהוָ֜ה כֹּ֣ל ׀ דְּמֵ֣י בֵית־שָׁא֗וּל
8.note: Shimei is using an expression similar to the one David used in 3:29 when he spoke of the blood of Abner being on the head of Joab. By saying that Yahweh has brought the blood of the house of Saul **upon** David, Shimei means that Yahweh is holding David responsible for shedding this blood and punishing him for doing that. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is holding you responsible for all of the blood of the house of Saul that you shed]

8.q: הֵשִׁיב֩ עָלֶ֨י⁠ךָ יְהוָ֜ה כֹּ֣ל ׀ דְּמֵ֣י בֵית־שָׁא֗וּל
8.note: Shimei is using **blood** to represent death, since people bleed when they are killed violently. He is referring to the many people whom David’s soldiers killed when, in order to make David the king, they fought against soldiers loyal to Saul’s descendants. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is holding you responsible for the deaths of all of the people loyal to Saul whom your soldiers killed]

Shimei is using the term **evil** to represent what he believes are the consequences of evil actions on David’s part. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And behold you suffering the consequences of your evil actions]

Shimei is using **behold you** as a common expression of his culture to mean that one can **behold** or look at David and see that what he is saying is true. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now look at you, suffering the consequences of your evil actions] or [It is clear that you are suffering the consequences of your evil actions]

9.q: לָ֣⁠מָּה יְקַלֵּ֞ל הַ⁠כֶּ֤לֶב הַ⁠מֵּת֙ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ
9.note: Abishai is using the question form for emphasis to express his outrage that Shimei would curse King David. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This dead dog should not be cursing my lord the king!]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:5. Alternate translation: [contemptible person]

Even though Abishai is addressing David directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **my lord the king** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [you, my lord the king]

10.note: David is using **What to me and to you** as a common expression of his culture to say that he has nothing in common with these **sons of Zeruiah** in terms of what they want to do. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will have nothing to do with your suggestion, sons of Zeruiah!]

The word **you** is plural here because David is addressing both Abishai and Joab. Joab seems to have been nearby and supporting his brother Abishai’s suggestion. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

10.q: כי יְקַלֵּ֗ל ו⁠כי יְהוָה֙ אָ֤מַר ל⁠וֹ֙ קַלֵּ֣ל אֶת־דָּוִ֔ד וּ⁠מִ֣י יֹאמַ֔ר מַדּ֖וּעַ עָשִׂ֥יתָה כֵּֽן
10.note: David is using the question form for emphasis to express that no one should tell Shimei that he should not curse David. He is suggesting that someone might use the question form to tell Shimei that. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for those purposes, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [If he is cursing me because Yahweh has said to him, ‘Curse David,’ then no one should tell him, ‘You should not be doing thus’!]

10.q: ו⁠כי יְהוָה֙ אָ֤מַר ל⁠וֹ֙ קַלֵּ֣ל אֶת־דָּוִ֔ד וּ⁠מִ֣י יֹאמַ֔ר מַדּ֖וּעַ עָשִׂ֥יתָה כֵּֽן
10.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [because Yahweh has told him to curse me, then no one should ask him why he is doing this] or [because Yahweh has told him to curse me, then no one should tell him that he should not be doing this]

David probably does not mean to suggest that Yahweh may have said this directly to Shimei. Instead, he probably means that Yahweh may have led Shimei to do this. So even if your language could put a quotation within a quotation, you may wish not to represent this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has led him to curse me]

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:12. Alternate translation: [whose actual father I am]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:8. Alternate translation: [is seeking to kill me]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:11. Alternate translation: [And with how much greater reason]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that now a Benjaminite should wish that I were dead]

13.note: The phrase **walking and he cursed** expresses a single idea. The word **cursed** tells in what way Shimei was **walking**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [walking cursingly] or [cursing as he walked]
See how you translated the similar expression in 16:6. Alternate translation: [and he threw stones at him]

It might seem that the expression **dusted with dust** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and he showered dirt on him]

Throwing dust on David was a symbolic action by which Shimei showed extreme disrespect and contempt for him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he threw dirt at him to show his contempt]

14.note: The implication is that David and his people arrived at the fords of the Jordan River. That was where David specified he would be going in 15:28. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [arrived at the fords of the Jordan]

15.note: The author is using **the people, a man of Israel** as a common expression of his culture to refer to Israelites from various tribes. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Israelites from various tribes who had joined him]

16.note: Hushai is repeating this phrase in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If speakers of your language repeat phrases for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [May the king live forever!]

Hushai is using a courteous and deferential expression that people in this culture would use to greet and acknowledge someone as their ruler. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Long live the king! Long live the king!] or [God save the king! God save the king!]

17.q: זֶ֥ה חַסְדְּ⁠ךָ֖ אֶת־רֵעֶ֑⁠ךָ לָ֥⁠מָּה לֹֽא־הָלַ֖כְתָּ אֶת־רֵעֶֽ⁠ךָ
17.note: Absalom is using the question form to express disappointment with Hushai and to rebuke him for not being loyal to David. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You are not showing loyalty to your friend! I would have expected you to go with him.]

18.note: Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [all the people of Israel]
See the discussion of this phrase in the Introduction to this chapter.

19.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use, or you could use a comparable expression. Alternate translation: [And point number two] or [Furthermore]

19.q: לְ⁠מִי֙ אֲנִ֣י אֶֽעֱבֹ֔ד הֲ⁠ל֖וֹא לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י בְנ֑⁠וֹ
19.note: Hushai is using the question form to emphasize that it is right and proper for him to serve Absalom, David’s son. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [it is appropriate for you, his son, to be the one before whose face I serve!]

After saying that Yahweh, the people present, and many other Israelites have chosen Absalom as king, Hushai is stating the pronoun **I**, even though its meaning is already included in the verb translated as **shall I serve**, to indicate that for his part, he will do the same thing. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that Hushai is saying that his own actions will be comparable to those of others. It may not be necessary to represent the separately stated pronoun explicitly. Alternate translation: [before whom shall I, for my part, serve]

19.q: הֲ⁠ל֖וֹא לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י בְנ֑⁠וֹ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָבַ֨דְתִּי֙ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ כֵּ֖ן אֶהְיֶ֥ה לְ⁠פָנֶֽי⁠ךָ
19.note: Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Is it not in the presence of his son? Just as I served in the presence of your father, thus I will be in your presence]

20.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֥אמֶר אַבְשָׁל֖וֹם אֶל־אֲחִיתֹ֑פֶל הָב֥וּ לָ⁠כֶ֛ם עֵצָ֖ה
20.note: The implied “you” in the imperative **Give** is plural, as the plural pronoun **yourselves** indicates. While the author says that Absalom spoke these words to Ahithophel, Absalom was evidently addressing him as chief among a group of advisors. So use a plural form of the imperative in your translation if your language marks that distinction. You may also wish to indicate more fully whom Absalom was addressing. Alternate translation: [And Absalom said to Ahithophel and his other advisors, “Give counsel for yourselves]

Absalom is using the pronoun **yourselves** because his advisors are part of the group for whose benefit this **counsel** will be given. Since the speaker, Absalom, is also part of this group, it may be natural in your language to use a first-person plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [Give counsel for us]

21.note: The author is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **Go in to**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [Sleep with]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:6. Alternate translation: [you have incensed your father] or [you have made yourself abhorrent to your father]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:7. Alternate translation: [and all who are with you will become more determined]

22.note: Here, the word **eyes** represents sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the sight of all of Israel]

The author says **all of Israel** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [for any Israelite to see]

23.q: וַ⁠עֲצַ֣ת אֲחִיתֹ֗פֶל אֲשֶׁ֤ר יָעַץ֙ בַּ⁠יָּמִ֣ים הָ⁠הֵ֔ם כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִשְׁאַל־בִּ⁠דְבַ֣ר הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֑ים
23.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what has just happened in the story. He is accounting for why Absalom did such an outrageous thing without questioning it. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

It might seem that the expression **counsel of Ahithophel that he counseled** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [Now the counsel that Ahithophel gave]

The author is using the term **word** to represent what God would say by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what God had to say]
